text: For kharif paddy nursery in Odisha, prepare raised seedbeds of 1.2 m width and convenient length. Treat seeds with Carbendazim at 2 g per kg seed or Trichoderma viride at 5 g per kg seed to prevent seed-borne blast and seedling blight before sowing.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: In paddy, transplant 20 to 25 days old seedlings with 2 to 3 seedlings per hill at a spacing of 20 cm by 15 cm in well-puddled fields. For SRI method (System of Rice Intensification), transplant single young seedlings of 10 to 12 days old with wider spacing of 25 cm by 25 cm.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Yellow stem borer in paddy causes dead hearts during the vegetative stage and white heads or white ears during panicle emergence. Monitor adult moths using light traps and pheromone traps at 8 traps per acre. Clip seedling leaf tips before transplanting to eliminate stem borer egg masses.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Rice

text: For chemical control of yellow stem borer in paddy when economic threshold level of 5 percent dead hearts is reached, apply Chlorantraniliprole 0.4 percent G at 4 kg per acre or Cartap hydrochloride 4 percent G at 7.5 kg per acre in standing water.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Rice

text: Brown Planthopper (BPH) attacks paddy by sucking plant sap from the base of tillers, leading to yellowing, drying, and characteristic hopper burn circular patches in the field. Maintain alleyways of 30 cm after every 2 meters of planting to allow aeration and light penetration.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Rice

text: To control Brown Planthopper (BPH) in paddy, avoid excessive nitrogenous fertilizers. Alternate wetting and drying in fields reduces nymphal survival. If population exceeds threshold of 5 to 10 hoppers per hill, spray Pymetrozine 50 percent WDG at 120 g per acre or Triflumezopyrim 10 percent SC at 94 ml per acre directed towards the base of the plant.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Rice

text: Paddy blast caused by Pyricularia oryzae produces spindle-shaped lesions with grey centres on leaves, and blackening around neck nodes causing panicle breakage (neck blast). Avoid heavy single doses of urea, maintain field hygiene, and spray Tricyclazole 75 percent WP at 120 g per acre or Kasugamycin 3 percent SL at 400 ml per acre at initial symptom appearance.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Bacterial leaf blight (BLB) of paddy causes dull green water-soaked lesions starting from leaf tips and margins, later turning straw-yellow with wavy margins. Drain stagnant water and reduce nitrogen fertilizer application. Spray Copper Oxychloride at 500 g plus Streptocycline at 6 g in 200 litres of water per acre.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Fertilizer management for medium duration high-yielding paddy in Odisha: Apply NPK in the ratio of 80:40:40 kg per hectare. Apply full dose of Phosphorus (SSP or DAP) and half dose of Potash (MOP) as basal application before final puddling. Apply Nitrogen in three equal split doses: one-third at basal, one-third at active tillering (21 days after transplanting), and one-third at panicle initiation.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Zinc deficiency in paddy causes khaira disease, showing reddish-brown rusty spots on lower leaves that coalesce and stunt crop growth. Apply Zinc Sulphate (21 percent Zn) at 10 kg per acre as basal soil application, or foliar spray 0.5 percent Zinc Sulphate with 0.25 percent slaked lime at tillering stage.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Water management in transplanted paddy: Maintain shallow standing water of 2 to 3 cm depth during the first week after transplanting to encourage root establishment. Increase water depth to 5 cm during tillering and panicle development. Practice alternate wetting and drying during vegetative growth to conserve water and improve root aeration.
source: Directorate of Agriculture and Food Production, Odisha

text: Drain all standing water from paddy fields 10 to 14 days before anticipated harvest date. Premature draining reduces grain filling and 1000-grain weight, while late draining delays harvest, hampers mechanized combine harvesting, and leads to lodging and grain sprouting in humid coastal conditions.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Harvest paddy when 80 to 85 percent of the panicles turn golden yellow and grain moisture is around 20 to 22 percent. Thresh immediately and sun-dry the paddy grains on a clean threshing floor or tarpaulin sheet until moisture drops to 12 to 14 percent for safe grain storage without mould or insect attack.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Weed management in direct seeded and transplanted paddy: Apply Pre-emergence herbicide Pretilachlor 50 percent EC at 600 ml per acre within 3 to 5 days after transplanting in saturated soil. For post-emergence control of broadleaf weeds and sedges at 20 to 25 days after transplanting, spray Bispyribac-sodium 10 percent SC at 80 ml per acre.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Kharif Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Tomato nursery seedbed management: Raise seedlings on 15 cm high beds with fertile soil mixed with well-rotted FYM and vermicompost. Sow certified seeds of high-yielding hybrid varieties like Utkal Deepti, Pusa Ruby, or Arka Rakshak at 100 to 150 g seeds per acre. Cover with thin layer of straw and irrigate with rose can.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: Damping off in tomato nursery causes seed rot and sudden falling over of seedlings at soil level due to Pythium and Rhizoctonia fungi under waterlogged conditions. Avoid overwatering, drench seedbed with Trichoderma harzianum at 10 g per litre or spray Copper Oxychloride 50 percent WP at 2.5 g per litre water.
source: OUAT Vegetable Production Manual, Bhubaneswar

text: Whiteflies on tomato are small winged sap-sucking insects clustering on the underside of leaves that transmit the debilitating Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (ToLCV). Leaves turn cupped, curled upward, stunted, and puckered. Install bright yellow sticky traps at plant canopy height at 15 to 20 traps per acre to monitor and trap adult whiteflies.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Solanaceous Crops

text: To control whitefly and reduce viral transmission in tomato, spray Neem oil (Azadirachtin 1500 ppm) at 3 to 5 ml per litre of water at early infestation. If pest pressure is severe, spray systemic insecticide Acetamiprid 20 percent SP at 0.5 g per litre or Imidacloprid 17.8 percent SL at 0.5 ml per litre in early morning or evening hours.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Solanaceous Crops

text: Early blight of tomato caused by Alternaria solani produces concentric ring spots resembling a target board on older leaves first, causing them to turn yellow and drop prematurely. Space plants 60 cm by 45 cm for good airflow, remove lower infected foliage, and spray Mancozeb 75 percent WP at 2 g per litre or Chlorothalonil 75 percent WP at 2 g per litre.
source: OUAT Vegetable Production Manual, Bhubaneswar

text: Integrated non-chemical control of tomato fruit borer (Helicoverpa armigera) includes installing sex pheromone traps (Helilure) at 5 traps per acre for pest monitoring, handpicking and destroying bored fruits, and planting African marigold as a trap crop around borders in a 1:16 ratio. These cultural and biological control practices target larvae boring into developing green and ripe fruits, which leave circular holes contaminated with fecal matter.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Solanaceous Crops

text: For bio-rational control of tomato fruit borer, spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) formulation at 1.5 g per litre or HaNPV (Helicoverpa nuclear polyhedrosis virus) at 250 LE per acre along with 0.1 percent jaggery in evening hours. For heavy infestation, spray Chlorantraniliprole 18.5 percent SC at 0.3 ml per litre with a 3-day harvest withholding period.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Solanaceous Crops

text: Blossom end rot in tomato is a physiological disorder causing dark, leathery, sunken patches at the blossom end of fruits. It is triggered by calcium deficiency coupled with fluctuating soil moisture and extreme heat. Maintain regular irrigation through drip systems and apply foliar spray of Calcium Nitrate at 5 g per litre during fruit set.
source: OUAT Vegetable Production Manual, Bhubaneswar

text: Fertilizer schedule for hybrid tomato in coastal Odisha: Apply 10 to 12 tonnes well-rotted FYM per acre during field preparation. Recommended NPK dose is 120:80:100 kg per hectare. Apply 50 percent Nitrogen and 100 percent of Phosphorus and Potash at transplanting. Top dress remaining 50 percent Nitrogen in two equal splits at 30 and 45 days after transplanting followed by earthing up.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: Irrigation management for tomato: Tomato is sensitive to waterlogging as well as severe drought stress which induces blossom drop and fruit cracking. Drip irrigation at 2 to 3 days interval saves 40 percent water and enhances marketable fruit yield. Avoid furrow irrigation wetting foliage to minimize fungal disease incidence.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: Staking indeterminate tomato plants with bamboo poles, wooden stakes, or trellis wire at 30 days after transplanting keeps foliage and developing fruits off the ground. Staking reduces fruit rot by 60 percent, improves sun exposure, facilitates spraying, and yields uniform grade fruit.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: Harvest tomato fruits at breaker or turning stage (when blossom end turns pink or red) for distant transportation and wholesale marketing. For local market consumption, harvest at firm pink-red ripe stage. Harvest fruits early in the morning by gentle twisting to keep calyx intact and store in ventilated plastic crates.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: For rabi onion nursery in Odisha, sow seeds between mid-October and mid-November using suitable varieties like Bhima Super, Bhima Shakti, Agrifound Light Red, or Arka Kalyan. Seed rate is 3 to 4 kg per acre. Treat seeds with Thiram or Captan at 2.5 g per kg seed before broadcasting on raised nursery beds.
source: NHRDF Onion Production Guidelines & OUAT

text: Transplant sturdy 45 to 50 days old onion seedlings into flat beds or broad bed furrows at a spacing of 15 cm between rows and 10 cm between plants. Avoid over-aged seedlings exceeding 60 days as they initiate premature bolting (flowering seed stalks) resulting in small split unmarketable bulbs.
source: NHRDF Onion Production Guidelines & OUAT

text: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) are slender tiny yellow-brown sucking insects that congregate in leaf sheaths and inner neck tissues. They scrape leaf surfaces and suck sap, producing silvery-white blotches that curl and wither leaf tips. Hot and dry weather promotes explosive thrips multiplication.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Onion and Garlic

text: To manage onion thrips, install blue or yellow sticky traps at 15 traps per acre. Overhead sprinkler irrigation washes nymphs off foliage and reduces populations. If thrips exceed 20 to 30 per plant, spray Spinosad 45 percent SC at 0.3 ml per litre or Fipronil 5 percent SC at 1 ml per litre with a non-ionic sticker agent like Sandovit at 0.5 ml per litre.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Onion and Garlic

text: Purple blotch (Alternaria porri) in onion produces sunken white flecks on leaves and seed stalks that rapidly enlarge into oval purple-brown lesions with yellowish halos. Foliage breaks over at lesion spots. Spray Mancozeb 75 percent WP at 2.5 g per litre or Tebuconazole 25.9 percent EC at 1 ml per litre along with sticker.
source: NHRDF Onion Production Guidelines & OUAT

text: Basal rot of onion caused by Fusarium oxysporum leads to progressive yellowing and curving of leaves from tips downward. Roots rot completely and basal plate displays white or pinkish fungal mycelium. Drench infected plots with Carbendazim 50 percent WP at 2 g per litre and rotate crops with non-allium species.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Integrated Pest Management for Onion and Garlic

text: Fertilizer requirement for onion in Odisha: Apply NPK at 100:50:80 kg per hectare along with 30 kg elemental Sulphur per hectare. Sulphur application significantly enhances pyruvic acid content, bulb pungency, firmness, and storage shelf-life. Apply full P, K, and Sulphur with 50 percent N at planting; top-dress remaining N at 30 and 45 days.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Rabi Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Irrigation scheduling for onion: Onion has shallow adventitious roots and requires frequent light irrigations at 7 to 10 days interval in winter, reducing to 4 to 6 days in hot March conditions. Critical stages sensitive to water stress are bulb initiation (30 to 40 days) and rapid bulb enlargement (60 to 75 days).
source: NHRDF Onion Production Guidelines & OUAT

text: Completely stop irrigation 10 to 15 days before onion harvesting. Withholding water allows outer scales to dry, promotes neck pinching, and prevents secondary root regrowth and fungal soft rotting during post-harvest storage.
source: NHRDF Onion Production Guidelines & OUAT

text: Harvest onion when 50 to 60 percent of top foliage naturally lodges or falls over (neck fall). Dig out bulbs carefully without mechanical bruising. Cure harvested bulbs with leaves in windrows under field shade for 3 to 5 days, then clip tops leaving 2 to 3 cm neck and dry further in a well-ventilated dry storage structure.
source: NHRDF Onion Production Guidelines & OUAT

text: Storage of onion bulbs in Odisha: Store cured onions in well-aerated bamboo-slat structures with raised wire mesh flooring at 25 to 30 degrees Celsius and 65 to 70 percent relative humidity. Sort regularly every 15 days to discard rotted or sprouting bulbs.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: Seed tuber selection for potato planting in Odisha: Use certified, healthy, disease-free seed tubers of recommended varieties like Kufri Jyoti, Kufri Pukhraj, Kufri Surya, or Kufri Chandramukhi. Optimal seed tuber size is 30 to 50 g weight with 30 to 40 mm diameter having 2 to 3 well-sprouted stout green eyes.
source: ICAR-CPRI Central Potato Research Institute Advisory

text: Before planting, remove cold-stored potato seed tubers and pre-sprout in diffused daylight under shade for 10 to 14 days until sprouts grow 1 cm long. Treat whole or cut tubers with Mancozeb 75 percent WP at 2.5 g per litre or Trichoderma viride at 5 g per litre for 10 minutes to prevent black scurf and seed piece decay.
source: ICAR-CPRI Central Potato Research Institute Advisory

text: Field preparation and planting potato: Plough soil deeply 3 to 4 times to achieve a fine crumbly tilth free from hard clods. Plant seed tubers at 60 cm row-to-row spacing and 20 cm tuber-to-tuber spacing at 5 to 7 cm depth on ridges. Seed rate is 10 to 12 quintals per acre for whole tubers.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Rabi Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Late blight of potato (Phytophthora infestans) is the most destructive disease causing water-soaked pale green lesions on leaves that rapidly turn purplish-brown with white downy mildew on leaf undersides under foggy, cool, humid conditions. When night temp is 10 to 15 C and RH exceeds 85 percent, late blight can destroy whole fields within 4 to 7 days.
source: ICAR-CPRI Potato Late Blight Management Bulletin

text: Management of potato late blight: Apply prophylactic protective spray of Mancozeb 75 percent WP at 2.5 g per litre before weather turns cloudy and foggy. Upon disease symptom appearance, switch immediately to systemic fungicides such as Cymoxanil 8 percent plus Mancozeb 64 percent WP at 3 g per litre or Metalaxyl 8 percent plus Mancozeb 64 percent WP at 2.5 g per litre.
source: ICAR-CPRI Potato Late Blight Management Bulletin

text: Potato aphid (Myzus persicae) acts as a high-efficiency vector spreading Potato Leaf Roll Virus (PLRV) and Potato Virus Y (PVY), causing leaf rolling, mosaic mottling, and drastic tuber yield loss. Monitor aphid populations with yellow water pan traps. If aphids exceed threshold of 20 aphids per 100 leaves in seed crop, spray Imidacloprid 17.8 percent SL at 0.3 ml per litre.
source: ICAR-CPRI Central Potato Research Institute Advisory

text: Earthing up (mitti chadhana) in potato: Perform first earthing up at 25 to 30 days after planting when plants reach 15 to 20 cm height. Build broad high ridges around plant bases to prevent sunlight exposure to developing tubers which turns them green and bitter due to toxic solanine alkaloid synthesis.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Rabi Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Fertilizer dose for potato in Odisha: Apply 12 to 15 tonnes well decomposed cowdung manure per acre. Recommended mineral fertilizer dose is 120 kg Nitrogen, 100 kg Phosphorus (P2O5), and 120 kg Potash (K2O) per hectare. Apply all P and K with half N at planting in furrows; top dress remaining half N during first earthing up.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Rabi Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Irrigation schedule for potato: First light irrigation should be given immediately after planting if soil is dry. Irrigate at 7 to 10 days interval ensuring water reaches half to two-thirds height of the ridge. Never allow water to overtop ridges as it causes soil crusting and tuber rotting. Critical stage is tuber bulking (45 to 70 days).
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Rabi Crops, Bhubaneswar

text: Dehaulming in potato: Cut down vegetative vines (haulms) at ground level 10 to 12 days before digging tubers. Dehaulming allows tuber skins to mature, cure, and harden, reducing skin peeling, bruising, and fungal infection during harvest, transit, and storage.
source: ICAR-CPRI Central Potato Research Institute Advisory

text: Harvesting and curing potato: Dig potato tubers when soil is friable and dry, taking care not to cut tubers with spades or tractor blades. Keep harvested tubers in heaps under shade for 10 to 15 days for skin curing. Grade tubers according to size and discard cut, rotten, or green tubers before bagging in hessian bags.
source: ICAR-CPRI Central Potato Research Institute Advisory

text: Cold storage guidelines for potato: Store seed potatoes at 2 to 4 degrees Celsius and 90 to 95 percent relative humidity to maintain dormancy and prevent sprouting. For table potatoes, maintain 8 to 10 degrees Celsius with CIPC sprout inhibitor treatment to prevent accumulation of reducing sugars that darken chips during frying.
source: ICAR-CPRI Central Potato Research Institute Advisory

text: Shoot and fruit borer (Leucinodes orbonalis) in brinjal: Larvae bore into tender shoots causing wilting and drooping shoot tips in early stages, and bore into fruits leaving round exit holes plugged with excreta. Clip and destroy wilted shoots weekly, install pheromone traps at 12 traps per acre, and spray Chlorantraniliprole 18.5 percent SC at 0.4 ml per litre.
source: OUAT Vegetable Production Manual, Bhubaneswar

text: Little leaf disease of brinjal is caused by phytoplasma transmitted by leafhopper vector (Hishimonus phycitis). Leaves become extremely small, yellow, bushy, and plants bear no fruit. Roguing and burning infected plants and controlling leafhoppers with Dimethoate 30 percent EC at 1.5 ml per litre is recommended.
source: OUAT Vegetable Production Manual, Bhubaneswar

text: Groundnut cultivation in Odisha: Grow high-yielding bunch varieties like TAG-24, Dharani, or Smruti in well-drained sandy loam soil with pH 6.0 to 7.5. Inoculate seeds with Rhizobium culture and Trichoderma before sowing. Apply Gypsum at 200 kg per acre in two splits: half at sowing and half at pegging (40 to 45 days) to ensure pod filling.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Oilseeds, Bhubaneswar

text: Tikka leaf spot of groundnut produces circular dark brown spots with yellow halos (Cercospora arachidicola) causing severe defoliation and yield reduction. Spray Mancozeb at 2 g per litre or Hexaconazole 5 percent EC at 1.5 ml per litre at first appearance of spots.
source: OUAT Package of Practices for Oilseeds, Bhubaneswar

text: Soil testing guidelines for farmers in Odisha: Collect soil samples in a zig-zag pattern across the field at 15 cm depth for arable crops, mix thoroughly, dry in shade, and submit 500 g composite sample to the nearest block Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or soil testing laboratory. Test for pH, electrical conductivity, organic carbon, and available NPK.
source: Directorate of Agriculture and Food Production, Odisha

text: Management of acid soils in Odisha: Acid red and laterite soils prevalent in Bhubaneswar and interior Odisha with pH below 5.5 suffer from Aluminium toxicity and low Phosphorus availability. Apply agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) or dolomite at 2 to 4 quintals per acre once in three years during land preparation to neutralize acidity and enhance nutrient uptake.
source: OUAT Soil Management Advisory Bulletin, Bhubaneswar

text: Vermicompost and Farmyard Manure (FYM) application: Incorporate 2 to 3 tonnes of well-decomposed FYM or 1 tonne of vermicompost per acre during final field ploughing 2 weeks prior to sowing. Organic manure enriches soil microbial biomass, improves water holding capacity in sandy soils, and enhances micronutrient availability.
source: OUAT Soil Management Advisory Bulletin, Bhubaneswar

text: Bio-fertilizer application: Inoculate cereal seeds with Azotobacter or Azospirillum at 200 g per 10 kg seed, and pulse/legume seeds with Rhizobium. Use Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) at 2 kg per acre mixed with 50 kg moist compost applied in soil to dissolve fixed soil phosphorus into plant-absorbable orthophosphate ions.
source: OUAT Soil Management Advisory Bulletin, Bhubaneswar

text: Pesticide spraying weather precautions: Never spray chemical insecticides or fungicides if rain is expected within the next 4 to 6 hours or if wind speed exceeds 15 km per hour. Wind causes chemical drift into non-target areas and rain washes away deposits, wasting inputs and polluting local waterways. Spray during calm hours in early morning or late afternoon.
source: IMD Agromet Advisory Service, Bhubaneswar

text: Heavy rainfall and cyclone preparedness in coastal Odisha: Upon IMD warning of depression or cyclone in Bay of Bengal, immediately clean drainage channels and dig field outlets to drain excess surface water. Postpone top-dressing of urea and pesticide sprays until fields are drained and weather clears.
source: IMD Agromet Advisory Service, Bhubaneswar

text: Heat wave protection for vegetable crops in April-May: High temperatures exceeding 38 degrees Celsius cause pollen sterility, flower dropping, and sunburn on tomato and brinjal fruits. Provide light and frequent evening irrigations, use straw mulching to conserve root zone moisture, and erect shade net nurseries for young seedlings.
source: IMD Agromet Advisory Service, Bhubaneswar

text: Foggy and overcast weather advisory: Continuous cloudy conditions with relative humidity above 85 percent and temperatures between 15 and 22 C create ideal conditions for fungal pathogens like late blight in potato and downy mildew. Farmers should inspect crop canopies daily and apply preventative protective sprays.
source: IMD Agromet Advisory Service, Bhubaneswar

text: Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE 5 percent) preparation: Pound 50 g dry neem seed kernels into coarse powder, tie in a muslin cloth, and soak in 1 litre of water overnight. Squeeze the pouch thoroughly and filter the milky extract. Add 1 ml mild soap detergent as emulsifier and spray immediately against aphids, whiteflies, and young caterpillar borers.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Farmer IPM Guide

text: Yellow and blue sticky traps for pest monitoring: Install bright yellow sticky traps at crop canopy height at 15 to 20 traps per acre to trap sucking pests like whiteflies and aphids. Blue sticky traps attract thrips. Check traps twice weekly to monitor pest population trends before deciding on chemical sprays.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Farmer IPM Guide

text: Pheromone traps for borer management: Use species-specific sex pheromone traps at 5 to 8 traps per acre for monitoring and 15 to 20 traps for mass trapping. Replace pheromone lures every 3 weeks. Pheromone traps disrupt mating and indicate peak moth flights, signaling exact timing for bio-agent or insecticide releases.
source: ICAR-NCIPM Farmer IPM Guide

text: Trichoderma bio-fungicide application: Trichoderma viride and Trichoderma harzianum are antagonist beneficial fungi that protect crops against seed rot, collar rot, and root wilt diseases. Apply 5 to 10 g per kg seed for seed treatment, or mix 1 kg Trichoderma with 100 kg moist farmyard manure, incubate for 7 days under shade, and broadcast in one acre before planting.
source: OUAT Bio-control Laboratory Advisory, Bhubaneswar

text: Drip irrigation benefits and maintenance for vegetables: Drip irrigation delivers water and water-soluble fertilizers directly to plant root zones, saving 40 to 60 percent water compared to flood irrigation while suppressing weed growth in inter-row spaces. Flush lateral lines fortnightly and clean disk filters weekly to prevent emitter clogging by silt and algae.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: Mulching for soil moisture conservation: Spread organic mulch such as clean paddy straw or sugarcane bagasse at 5 tonnes per acre or 25 to 30 micron silver-black plastic mulch over vegetable planting beds. Mulching conserves 30 to 50 percent soil moisture, reduces soil temperature fluctuations, and inhibits weed emergence.
source: Directorate of Horticulture, Govt of Odisha

text: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) guidelines in Odisha: Farmers must enroll their crops on the national crop insurance portal or through local primary agricultural credit societies (PACS) before cut-off dates: July 31 for Kharif crops and December 31 for Rabi crops. Farmers pay nominal premium of 2 percent for kharif food grains and 1.5 percent for rabi crops.
source: Department of Agriculture and Farmers' Empowerment, Govt of Odisha

text: Selling agricultural produce at Minimum Support Price (MSP): Registered farmers can sell paddy and other notified crops at government procurement centres (mandis) by registering on the farmer registration portal (e-Samiksha / e-Paddy procurement). Farmers receive payment directly into their Aadhaar-linked bank accounts through DBT within 24 to 48 hours of sale.
source: Odisha State Civil Supplies Corporation (OSCSC)

text: Kisan Call Centre (KCC) and Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) advisory services: Farmers can call the toll-free national Kisan Call Centre number 1800-180-1551 from 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM on all days to seek free agricultural advisory in their local language from farm scientists. District KVK scientists also organize on-farm diagnostic field visits.
source: Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, Govt of India

text: Paddy grain storage against storage pests: Fumigate clean storage godowns before storing fresh paddy. Maintain grain moisture below 12 percent. Mix 1 kg dry neem leaves or inert clay dust per 100 kg grain, or use airtight Hermetic storage bags (PICS bags) to suffocate rice weevils (Sitophilus oryzae) without chemical residues.
source: OUAT Department of Entomology, Bhubaneswar

text: Safe handling and protective equipment for agricultural pesticides: Always wear protective masks, rubber gloves, goggles, and long-sleeved clothing while measuring and spraying chemical pesticides. Never spray against wind direction, never blow clogged spray nozzles with mouth, and wash spraying equipment and clothing thoroughly after application away from drinking water wells.
source: Central Insecticides Board & Registration Committee (CIBRC)
